# Population geometry controls the rank of the learning source

Internal derivation, 2026-09-30. This is a continuation of the same functional-population encoding question. It addresses the user's clarified contract: an autonomous two-order approximation with O(Lnpq+nd) evolving learned state, where p compresses the input population and q compresses time history. A dense trained driver is forbidden. This note proves a source approximation result, not the full autonomous trajectory theorem.

## 1. Compress the interaction generated by the population

For the canonical squared-loss flow at hidden layer l>=2, define

\[
G_l(\theta)=\frac1n E_\mu[r_\theta(x)\delta_l(\theta,x)h_{l-1}(\theta,x)^T],
\qquad \dot W_l=-2G_l(\theta).
\tag{1}
\]

Here y=f*(x), or more generally the expectation may be over (x,y). The residual is r=f-y, excluding the residual from delta. For one current state, set

\[
a(x,y)=r(x,y)\delta_l(x)/\sqrt n,\qquad
b(x)=h_{l-1}(x)/\sqrt n.
\]

Then G=E[ab^T]. This is the **current gradient source**, not the trained matrix and not an individual neuron's entire input function. A population of arbitrarily many examples can generate a source of modest approximate rank even when its individual response fields require many input coordinates.

The proposed population order is therefore the number of paired directions needed to represent G. These directions will be recomputed from the current compressed network, so they need not remain in their initial neuron-space span. The initialized hidden matrices are retained exactly throughout.

## 2. A general elementary source-tail lemma

Let b:X->R^n be measurable, square-integrable and L_b-Lipschitz from a metric space (X,d_X) into ordinary Euclidean norm, and let a be measurable with E||a||_2^2 <= A_2^2. Define the squared p-center distortion of the input marginal mu by

\[
Q_p(\mu)=\inf_{c_1,\ldots,c_p\in X}
E_\mu\min_{1\le j\le p}d_X(x,c_j)^2.
\tag{2}
\]

For every p>=1 there is a rank-at-most-2p matrix G_{2p} such that

\[
\|G-G_{2p}\|_F
\le A_2L_b\sqrt{Q_p(\mu)/(p+1)}.
\tag{3}
\]

If the infimum is not attained, the statement follows by taking arbitrarily close center sets and then using continuity of the best rank-2p error. If 2p>=n, exact representation gives zero error. Finite empirical and continuous input laws are both allowed.

**Proof.** Choose p centers and assign each input to a nearest-center cell, breaking ties measurably. Let b_bar(x)=E[b|cell(x)]. Conditional expectation minimizes mean square error among cell-constant vectors, hence

\[
E\|b-b_{\rm bar}\|_2^2
\le E\|b(x)-b(c_{\operatorname{cell}(x)})\|_2^2
\le L_b^2 E\min_jd_X(x,c_j)^2.
\tag{4}
\]

Split

\[
G=C+R,\quad C=E[ab_{\rm bar}^T]
=\sum_j\mu(C_j)E[a|C_j]E[b|C_j]^T,
\quad R=E[a(b-b_{\rm bar})^T].
\]

The first matrix has rank at most p. A rank-one matrix uv^T has nuclear norm ||u|| ||v||, so triangle inequality and Cauchy--Schwarz give

\[
\|R\|_*\le E[\|a\|\,\|b-b_{\rm bar}\|]
\le A_2L_b\big(E\min_jd_X(x,c_j)^2\big)^{1/2}.
\tag{5}
\]

Let R_p retain its largest p singular values. With singular values sigma_j in descending order,

\[
\|R-R_p\|_F^2
=\sum_{j>p}\sigma_j^2
\le\sigma_{p+1}\sum_{j>p}\sigma_j
\le\|R\|_*^2/(p+1).
\tag{6}
\]

Thus G_{2p}=C+R_p has rank at most 2p and satisfies (3). This proof does not differentiate a, the backward response, or the teacher. It uses the rough factor only through its L2 magnitude and uses geometric regularity only on the forward factor.

The extra factor p^(-1/2) comes from compressing the remaining cross interaction after the coarse geometric approximation. It is not a claim that a p-cell quadrature rule itself has this faster integration error. In particular G_{2p} is not generally the gradient on those p centers. The centers prove a spectral-tail bound; the eventual algorithm may approximate the source spectrum without storing any such input grid.

## 3. Width-uniform specialization to canonical deep training

Assume bounded phi and phi', zero readout, ||x||/sqrt(d)<=R, and E y^2=Y^2<infinity. Work on [0,T] and an initialization event

\[
\max_{l\ge2}\|W_l(0)\|_{op}\le K_0,
\qquad \|W_1(0)\|_{op}/\sqrt n\le K_1.
\tag{7}
\]

For fixed input dimension d these constants can be chosen independently of width at any fixed confidence under canonical Gaussian initialization. If d also grows, the first bound K1 necessarily accounts for sqrt(d/n); n>=d is one sufficient way to keep it bounded. This note claims width uniformity, not uniformity over arbitrary ratios d/n.

Use the normalized input metric d_X(x,x')=||x-x'||/sqrt(d). The exact loss dissipation identity gives a parameter-path length at most V=Y sqrt(T) in the metric with first weights/readout divided by sqrt(n). Therefore

\[
\|W_l(t)\|_{op}\le Q:=K_0+V,\qquad
\|W_1(t)\|_{op}/\sqrt n\le K_1+V,\qquad
\|w(t)\|_2/\sqrt n\le V.
\tag{8}
\]

Write A=||phi'||_infty. Forward subtraction through the A-Lipschitz activation gives

\[
\frac{\|h_j(t,x)-h_j(t,x')\|_2}{\sqrt n}
\le L_{b,j}\,d_X(x,x'),\quad
L_{b,j}=A^jQ^{j-1}(K_1+V).
\tag{9}
\]

Backward propagation in normalized Euclidean norm gives

\[
\sup_x\|\delta_l(t,x)\|_2/\sqrt n
\le D_l:=A^{L-l+1}Q^{L-l}V,
\qquad \|a\|_{L^2}\le D_l\rho(t),
\tag{10}
\]

where rho=(E r^2)^(1/2)<=Y. These are RMS bounds; no trained coordinatewise Gaussian tail bound is used.

Substituting (9)--(10) in (3) proves

\[
\inf_{\operatorname{rank} Z\le2p}\|G_l(t)-Z\|_F
\le D_l\rho(t)L_{b,l-1}\sqrt{Q_p(\mu)/(p+1)}.
\tag{11}
\]

The constant is uniform in n, training-sample count, and t<=T. This is a source approximation theorem for every hidden layer at fixed depth. It neither assumes the source is exactly low rank nor asserts the same singular spectrum for the accumulated trained matrix.

The same algebra applies to any current compressed physical state satisfying (8) and the stated residual bound. However, (8) for an autonomous finite-history closure needs its own stability/continuation argument. Dense-flow energy cannot simply be assigned to that closure.

## 4. A transparent data class and its rate

Suppose the input law admits

\[
Q_p(\mu)^{1/2}\le D p^{-1/s}
\tag{12}
\]

with fixed D,s. This is an assumption about the **input distribution's geometric complexity**, not about the density being polynomial. It is satisfied, for example, by a bounded Lipschitz image of a fixed s-dimensional cube, including finitely many such charts, with constants accounting for the charts. To verify it directly, partition each parameter cube into k^s subcubes. A Lipschitz image maps each cell to diameter at most C/k; choose one image center per cell and k=floor(p^(1/s)), adjusting a fixed constant for small p and multiple charts. The bound holds for any probability law supported on that image, so no smooth density is required.

Under (12), after absorbing the factor two between p and retained rank,

\[
\inf_{\operatorname{rank}Z\le p}\|G_l(t)-Z\|_F
\le C_{L,T}\rho(t)\,p^{-\beta},
\qquad \beta=\tfrac12+\tfrac1s.
\tag{13}
\]

Examples: curve support gives beta=3/2; surface support beta=1; intrinsic dimension three gives beta=5/6. For a generic full d-dimensional cube, this sufficient bound has s=d; for a full sphere, s is its intrinsic dimension. Thus this theorem does not erase the curse for every high-dimensional distribution. It avoids an ambient-dimensional exponent when the data have low intrinsic geometry, even if their ambient vectors are large and the support contains infinitely many inputs.

No teacher differentiability is needed for (13), only finite label second moment. Conversely, a smooth or one-index teacher on a full high-dimensional input distribution does not imply (12). Whether teacher structure yields a faster *task-weighted* source spectrum without low-dimensional input geometry is a separate open question.

## 5. Autonomous implementation target and what remains unproved

At each current compressed state compute a factorized source approximation G_l,p=A_l B_l^T with n-by-p factors. Their actions can be obtained without forming G_l:

\[
G_l V=\frac1n E[r\delta_l(h_{l-1}^TV)],\qquad
G_l^T U=\frac1n E[rh_{l-1}(\delta_l^TU)].
\tag{14}
\]

All responses in (14) come from the current compressed network. Accumulate q temporal moments of each column of A_l and B_l and pair matching temporal modes to reconstruct the learned matrix. This gives an autonomous candidate with O(Lnpq+nd+Lp^2) learned state, described explicitly in INTERACTION_BASIS_ROUTE.md. It does not store a dense trained oracle. Population integration is performed as streamed deterministic averages or sampled expectations, with its numerical error and work counted separately.

Equation (13) bounds the optimal source tail. It does **not** by itself prove:

1. that a particular current-state matrix-free factorization attains that tail uniformly along its own adaptive trajectory;
2. that its factor histories have uniform q-approximation constants as p increases or regularization decreases;
3. that compression errors are amplified by only a width-independent factor through autonomous deep training;
4. an all-time theorem, or convergence to a canonical infinite-width predictor at a specified width rate.

These are the remaining bridges. A direct SVD truncation may have discontinuous factor choices near singular-value crossings. A ridge factorization makes the source factors smooth but introduces regularization-dependent constants that must be included in the complexity comparison. A future proof must not set those constants to one.

## 6. The actual criterion for a compression advantage

For clarity, suppose a future full theorem establishes

\[
\sup_{t\le T}\|\hat f_{n,p,q}(t)-f_n(t)\|_{L^2(\mu)}
\le C_T(p^{-\beta}+q^{-\alpha})
\tag{15}
\]

with C_T independent of n,p,q. Equation (15) is a **target**, not a consequence already proved by (13). At fixed accuracy epsilon, choose p~epsilon^(-1/beta), q~epsilon^(-1/alpha). Then

\[
S_{\rm learned}=O\bigl(Ln\epsilon^{-1/\beta-1/\alpha}+nd+L\epsilon^{-2/\beta}\bigr).
\tag{16}
\]

At a common chosen width n, strict subquadratic hidden learned state requires p q=o(n), or epsilon^(-1/beta-1/alpha)=o(n). The p-squared workspace is then dominated by npq. If total learned state includes the nd first layer, also require d=o(n), as holds for fixed input dimension. If one separately has a dense population approximation width n~epsilon^(-2), the sufficient exponent condition becomes

\[
1/\beta+1/\alpha<2.
\tag{17}
\]

For alpha=2 this requires beta>2/3. The proved source exponents in (13) meet that numerical threshold when s<6. For alpha=1 it requires beta>1, met by the curve case s=1. These are **feasibility calculations**, not established model-complexity theorems: the constants and the rate in (15), and the dense width rate, still have to be justified under the same hypotheses. A claim that fixed p,q gives linear width state alone would not prove matched-accuracy savings.

The mathematical advance in this note is (3)/(11): the learning source can be spectrally simpler than a full field reconstruction would suggest, and only one side of the paired population interaction needs geometric regularity to obtain the extra p^(-1/2) factor.
